The surest indication that Anthony Albanese knows he has a mighty challenge on his hands in stalling Pauline Hanson was the timing of his major childcare policy this week, announced on the day the One Nation leader gave her first speech to the National Press Club.

Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh revealed in an ABC radio interview that the decision to extend the 15 per cent pay-rise subsidy for early educators and care workers was not provided for in the May budget and the decision was taken since, to be covered in the midyear update.

The cost of extending the subsidy for another two years is $3.6 billion. It comes with caps on fee increases and is to the benefit of one million families. Albanese bristled when he was asked if it was such a big deal.

“It sure is,” he told a sceptical journalist, “because this is a program of increased funding that never happened previously.”

The pay-rise subsidy was introduced in 2024 and was due to run out in November. It stemmed the exodus of workers from the sector who were, according to their union, “underpaid and exhausted”.

Hanson’s reaction at the National Press Club couldn’t have been more suited to the government’s purpose had Labor scripted it for her.

She disparaged the need for early educators to have a degree and said the entire annual $16 billion system is “out of proportion” and needs a thorough investigation. “I was a mother of four children,” she said. “I didn’t have a university degree to look after my children.”

Her shameless ignorance of advances in childhood education was of a piece with her complete disregard for the complexities of the energy crisis, her disregard for the “hoax” science of climate change and her glib promise to dismantle renewable energy programs to deliver cheaper plentiful electricity by building new coal-fired power stations in South Australia and Queensland and a nuclear power plant on the east coast.

If necessary, a Hanson government would have taxpayers foot the bill, but she is open to private capital joining the mission.

Hanson’s major donor, Gina Rinehart, who she admitted in a recent ABC radio interview gives her policy advice as well as the million-dollar plane and other generous emoluments, would have been very pleased indeed.

Hanson says the plane saves taxpayers money, which suggests she is either oblivious to perceptions of potentially corrupt influence or just doesn’t care. One rule for her and another for everyone else.

Hanson’s confidence is palpable, no doubt bolstered by her party’s remarkable rise in the opinion polls. The Resolve poll in The Age further fed this hubris when, for the first time, it asked respondents to say whom they would prefer as prime minister: Albanese, Angus Taylor or Hanson.

Hanson came in first, with 33 per cent of voters; 29 per cent nominated Albanese, and only 16 per cent preferred the Liberal leader. Twenty-two per cent were undecided.

The posing of this question throws a spotlight on the role of the legacy media in not only jumping on board her bandwagon but actively helping to propel it.

Newspoll and Resolve, for example, do not publish two-party preferred results. Their news coverage, which mightily drives the narrative, is shaped by the primary vote results. This ignores that Australia has a preferential voting system.

The Roy Morgan poll acknowledges this and so far it has found that Labor after preferences would retain government through the recent Hanson surge.

Polling analyst Kevin Bonham applies a two-party preferred result based on the data of Resolve and Newspoll, and has similarly found that Labor has retained its election-winning lead.

Hanson’s performance at the National Press Club spooked some leading Liberals, with one texting that she “won today”. They were already down in the dumps, as the published polls this week have the Coalition trailing a bad third on the primaries.

Simon Crean was Labor leader between 2001 and 2003. At that time, as today, Newspoll only reported primary votes, and it was the party’s weaker primary vote that was seized on by his factional opponents to topple him. A former staffer says the two-party preferred poll had Crean leading.

Hanson is in the Senate. By convention, the prime minister is the leader of the party or parties who have the confidence of the House of Representatives. She is aware of this convention but earlier this month said she could be prime minister from the Senate.

Liberal John Gorton remained a senator for three weeks in 1968 after he was appointed party leader to replace the missing Harold Holt. He resigned from the Senate and successfully won a byelection for the seat of Higgins.

Gorton was not of a mind to overturn the principles in place since Federation. Hanson is keeping her options open.

Conventions last only as long as they are observed, as we saw in the 1975 blocking of supply by the Fraser Coalition.

Constitutional experts point out that there is not even a mention of the office of prime minister in the Constitution. However, as Anne Twomey notes, by established constitutional practice the government is formed in the House of Representatives. How a prime minister permanently in the Senate would function is open to speculation.

That prime minister could be challenged in the High Court on the argument that they were not fulfilling the obligation to be directly answerable to the House by way of Question Time, et cetera, but Twomey is not convinced the High Court would hear such a matter.

Former attorney-general Mark Dreyfus concedes it would be possible for a PM to be in the Senate and adds that the “current lot of right-wingers in Australia want to blow everything up”.

What could deter Hanson from the option is the mathematical fact that no matter how well One Nation does at the next half-Senate election, it will not gain a majority in the Senate. This means she would be given a much harder time there than if she was leading either a majority One Nation government or some form of coalition with the Liberals and Nationals in the lower house.

Hanson’s performance at the National Press Club spooked some leading Liberals, with one texting that she “won today”.

They were already down in the dumps, as the published polls this week have the Coalition trailing a bad third on the primaries. They have also lost one of their high-profile performers, Senator Jonno Duniam, who announced he is quitting politics by the end of the year.

This immediately prompted the media observation that Duniam “was a rat deserting the sinking ship”. This is something he and his leader, Angus Taylor, reject. There are genuine family reasons for his early retirement.

Labor’s Murray Watt says what was on display at the National Press Club was unvarnished Hanson putting her vision “for a more divided, more chaotic Australia that will send a shiver up the spine of every Australian worker”. He said what we saw was Hanson saying it is too hard to sack workers in Australia “at a time when people desperately need to hang on to their jobs to pay their bills”.

YouGov pollster Paul Smith says his poll’s finding of a surge in One Nation’s primary vote among working-class voters is no fluke. He says it constitutes “a fundamental redrawing of the electoral map in Australia”. Whether these voters are even aware of Hanson’s long-held antipathy to the Fair Work Commission is a moot point. Lower-income people voting against their own interests is a feature of populist ascendancies, most recently reflected in Donald Trump’s success in America.

Hanson dismissed the impact of the Iran war on energy costs and inflation and said the government “should stop blaming the Middle East”.

This is something the Reserve Bank of Australia’s Monetary Policy Board didn’t do on Tuesday. The board acknowledged that resolution of the conflict is “at an early stage”.

The board’s statement was a real dampener on confidence: “There are plausible scenarios where inflation is higher and activity is lower than envisaged under the May baseline forecasts.” Chillingly, it added: “Global oil supply issues will take some time to resolve, maintaining upward pressure on global energy prices and inflation.”

Donald Trump’s seeming rupture with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu throws even more uncertainty into the mix. The president’s suggestion that Syria should be left to deal with Hezbollah “if Israel can’t do the job without killing everyone else” may have been tailored to his audience of European leaders at the Group of Seven, but it now remains to be seen how Israel reacts.

That response will be as relevant for Australians’ fuel security and cost-of-living struggles as it is for neighbouring countries in the Middle East, something Albanese emphasised in welcoming the announcement of a ceasefire.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers welcomed the Reserve Bank’s decision to leave rates at 4.35 per cent. He noted it was the first interest rates decision since his “responsible budget”, which he said improved the bottom line while still providing help with the cost of living.

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said Pauline Hanson still had some questions to answer, such as what seat will she run in if she wants to be prime minister and who will be her key ministers, because those appointments will impact Australians and their lives.

Who would have thought it could come to this?

Paul Bongiorno is a columnist for The Saturday Paper and a 35-year veteran of the Canberra Press Gallery.
